extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of literature, philosophy, and Plato; readers of literary criticism and political theory
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts standards for judging the value and social role of poetry, art, and related political-educational institutions, mainly in light of Plato's criticisms and the author's commentary. Useful for assessing literary purpose, moral effect, and civic functions of art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry as imitation and potential falsehood
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato’s charge that poets and the imitative arts are 'representatives of falsehood and feigning' — 'the false priests, false prophets, lying spirits, enchanters of the world.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat imitative art skeptically when it purports to convey ultimate truth; assess whether a poem merely imitates appearances or whether it carries genuine insight. Anti-patterns: art that substitutes mere semblance for truth or deliberately promotes error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poets' political complicity (flattery and patronage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato accuses poets of being 'friends of the tyrant, and bask in the sunshine of his patronage,' serving despotism by corrupting literature and morals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate poets for political alignment or servility: does the work flatter power, promote propaganda, or otherwise serve tyrannical interests? Examples: court poets who praise rulers; anti-pattern: time-serving verse that sacrifices moral independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional power of art — enlist feeling for reason
rubrics_metrics.description: The vocation of art is 'to present thought in the form of feeling, to enlist the feelings on the side of reason, to inspire even for a moment courage or resignation; perhaps to suggest a sense of infinity and eternity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value works that integrate feeling and thought — that move readers emotionally while reinforcing rational or ethical insight. Beware art that merely excites base passions without moral or intellectual direction. Assess whether emotion is moderated and educative rather than indulgent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between ideal truth and representational exactness
rubrics_metrics.description: All imitative art is 'subject to certain limitations' and involves a compromise: 'Something of ideal truth is sacrificed for the sake of the representation, and something in the exactness of the representation is sacrificed to the ideal.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating art, judge how well the work negotiates trade-offs between fidelity to particulars and expressive/idealised truth. Good practice: maintain a plausible or convincing representation while conveying a larger, essential truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permanent or enduring element of art (idealization and mediation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Works of art 'have a permanent element; they idealize and detain the passing thought, and are the intermediates between sense and ideas.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a work elevates transient experience into a form that communicates lasting insight. Look for artistic choices that distill or universalize experience rather than merely recording ephemeral detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Serious purpose and formative influence of literature
rubrics_metrics.description: The author echoes Plato’s concern about 'want of serious purpose in modern fiction,' arguing for an atmosphere where 'the beauty which meets the sense like a breeze and imperceptibly draws the soul... into harmony with the beauty of reason.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge literature on whether it serves an educative or morally formative role (especially for youth). Anti-patterns: frivolous, extravagant, or purely sensational works that lack a guiding ethical/intellectual aim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal poetry: hymn of divine perfection and civic good
rubrics_metrics.description: A desirable poetry would be 'the hymn of divine perfection, the harmony of goodness and truth among men' that 'would find materials in the living present as well as in the romance of the past,' 'elicit the simple principles... of truth and justice,' and 'preserve all the good of each generation and leave the bad unsung.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this composite ideal as a yardstick: does a poem unify goodness and truth, address present life and historical memory, extract essential moral/practical principles, and ennoble readers? Components to check include moral horizon, relevance, selectivity (unsung bad), and clarity of human insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry should furnish ideals of truth and action (not only aesthetic life-as-art)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrasting poets like Shakespeare (who 'has taught us how great men should speak and act') with Goethe (who 'furnishes no ideals of truth and action'), the text values poetry that gives models for conduct and moral imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor works that provide exemplars of character and action, not merely cultivated depictions of life. Anti-pattern: art that treats existence solely as aesthetic performance without offering ethical directions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagination is indispensable but must be guided
rubrics_metrics.description: Although Plato argues against dangerous degeneracy, the author insists 'to banish imagination wholly would be suicidal as well as impossible' — imagination distinguishes humans from animals and transforms thought into feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the role of imagination positively while checking for excesses that detach imagery from ethical or intellectual grounding. Good art combines imaginative richness with disciplined purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Storytelling craft: verisimilitude through natural touches
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrative of Er gains credibility from 'touches of nature' — precise coincidences, plausible timings, and realistic little details that an author like Defoe would use 'to win credibility for marvels and apparitions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess prose/fiction on its use of concrete, plausible detail to make extraordinary events believable. Scoring notes: look for specific sensory or circumstantial details that lend authenticity to the narrative world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom, choice, and the role of knowledge in virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: The text asserts 'The freedom of the will to refuse the evil and to choose the good is distinctly asserted' and that 'the routine of good actions and good habits is an inferior sort of goodness... he must add to virtue knowledge, if he is to act rightly when placed in new circumstances.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating moral education (in literature or philosophy), emphasize whether characters or systems cultivate knowledge-based virtue (reflective understanding) rather than mere habit. Anti-pattern: moralizing that reduces virtue to rote behavior without reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradoxes of the Republic as social/political design criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: The Republic presents several paradoxical institutional prescriptions identified as key features: (a) the community of property; (b) community of families; (c) the rule of philosophers; (d) the close analogy of the individual and the State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these listed paradoxes as evaluation axes when considering Platonic political designs: test practicality, moral justification, social consequences, and tension with modern notions of property, family, and governance. The author notes these are meant as ideals/patterns rather than practical blueprints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spartan and Pythagorean institutional features in the ideal State
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato’s ideal State borrows Spartan features (prohibition of gold and silver, common meals, military training of youth, state-regulated marriage and education, emphasis on physical well-being) and Pythagorean elements (rule of life, moral/intellectual training, importance of music and mathematics, mystical numbers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing a proposed civic or educational regimen, check for these institutional elements and evaluate their effects on discipline, equality, cultural formation, and potential repression. Examples and cautions are given (e.g., Spartan severity, Pythagorean exaggeration of music's influence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Community of property: practical and moral implications
rubrics_metrics.description: The community of goods (especially for guardians) is criticized by Aristotle and the author as tending to repress industry and benevolence, but is defended as conceivable in other historical/social contexts and not inherently impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat proposals for communal property as a criterion to be weighed on grounds of expediency, social consequences, historical precedent, and educational aims. Scoring should consider likely effects on motivation, distribution of benefits, and cultural adaptability.
